We are a team of curious and passionate innovators participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Our challenge is Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data. We aim to combine creativity, technology, and teamwork to develop innovative solutions for sustainable agriculture. We welcome enthusiastic members skilled in coding, data analysis, research, agriculture, UI/UX design, and creative problem-solving. Let's explore ideas
summary: FieldLoom AI, built by Team Lunar Elaris for the "Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data" challenge, is an explainable, multi-season crop rotation planner. Climate change is shifting rainfall and temperature patterns, and farmers must plan several seasons ahead, yet most tools only show weather or suggest a single crop. FieldLoom AI retrieves NASA POWER data for a farm's location and combines it with soil information, crop traits and farmer priorities. It calculates environmental indicators, scores crop suitability using transparent weights, and compares alternative four-season rotations such as Rice, Green gram, Maize and Cowpea. A climate what-if simulator lets users test hypothetical changes like lower rainfall or higher temperature. Every recommendation comes with a "Why This Recommendation?" explanation, and all data is labelled as observed, derived, assumed or hypothetical. Missing data lowers confidence instead of being guessed. Scores support decisions and are not yield predictions. Farmers can download a planning report, and the design allows more NASA datasets, such as GPM, SMAP and HLS, to be added later.
details:
FieldLoom AI is a web application that turns NASA Earth observation data and local farm information into transparent, multi-season crop rotation plans. A farmer creates a farm profile with location, soil type, pH, drainage, irrigation and crop history. Unknown soil values can be marked "Not available" instead of guessed. The app then retrieves real NASA POWER data for that location, including temperature, rainfall, humidity, wind and solar radiation, and calculates indicators such as monthly and seasonal rainfall, temperature trends and rainfall variability. A crop suitability engine scores each crop from a crop knowledge database using configurable weights for temperature, rainfall, water availability, soil and season. The rotation planner then builds and compares alternative four-season sequences, considering crop family diversity, repeated-crop risk, water demand, nutrient management and farmer priorities. A climate what-if simulator lets users test hypothetical changes such as lower rainfall, higher temperature or reduced irrigation, and a downloadable report summarizes everything.

The main benefit is clear, explainable decision support. Every recommendation includes a "Why This Recommendation?" panel describing which indicators, soil properties, crop traits, constraints and assumptions were used. Farmers can adjust their priorities, such as water saving or soil care, and see rankings update instantly.

The intended impact is to help farmers, starting with regions like Kerala, India, plan for changing rainfall and temperature patterns and use water more wisely. Because the design is modular, it can scale to other regions and datasets.

We built the frontend with React, Tailwind CSS, Recharts and Leaflet maps, and the backend with Python and FastAPI, using Pandas and NumPy for data processing and a database for saved farms and cached data. Each dataset is a separate provider module, so NASA GPM, SMAP, Landsat/Sentinel-2 (HLS) and NASA GIBS map layers can be added without changing the core engines.

The project is creative because it focuses on multi-season rotation planning rather than a single-crop recommendation or weather dashboard, and it combines scientific data with plain-language explanations. Honesty is built in: all data is labelled observed, derived, assumed or hypothetical, missing data lowers confidence, and sample data is always marked as demo data.

Our team considered data accuracy, spatial resolution limits, farmer usability, transparency and responsible communication. Suitability scores are decision support, not yield predictions, and the tool has not yet been scientifically validated. Next steps include validation with agronomists and local extension services.

If your app currently uses only NASA POWER, tell me and I'll adjust the wording so it only claims what is live.
